module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 364

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/364](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat

namespace Erdos364

/-- There is no consecutive triple of powerful numbers. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_364 :
    ¬ ∃ (n : ℕ), Powerful n ∧ Powerful (n + 1) ∧ Powerful (n + 2) := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős [Er76d] conjectured a stronger statement: if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number,
then $n_{k+2} - n_k > n_k^c$ for some constant $c > 0$.

[Er76d] Erdős, P., Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_364.variants.strong :
    ∃ (c : ℝ) (h : c > 0), ∀ (k : ℕ),
    Nat.nth Powerful (k + 2) - Nat.nth Powerful k > (Nat.nth Powerful k : ℝ) ^ c := by
  sorry

/--
There is no quadruple of powerful numbers, since at least one of the four numbers must be
$2 \pmod{4}$, which cannot be powerful (since $2$ divides it, but $2^2$ does not).
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_364.variants.weak :
    ¬ ∃ (n : ℕ), Powerful n ∧ Powerful (n + 1) ∧ Powerful (n + 2) ∧ Powerful (n + 3) := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := h
  have h2mod4 : n % 4 = 2 ∨ (n + 1) % 4 = 2 ∨ (n + 2) % 4 = 2 ∨ (n + 3) % 4 = 2 := by omega
  rcases h2mod4 with (_|_|_|_) <;>
  simp_all [not_full_of_prime_mod_prime_sq _ 1 (Nat.prime_two)]

end Erdos364

findings.description: The docstring at line 51 says “There is no quadruple of powerful numbers,” omitting “consecutive.” Literally this is false: 4, 8, 9, and 16 are four distinct powerful numbers. The Lean statement correctly rules out only n, n+1, n+2, n+3, so the formal mathematics is intact.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/364 explicitly says: “It is trivial that there are no quadruples of consecutive powerful numbers since one must be 2 (mod 4).”
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to “There is no quadruple of consecutive powerful numbers, since …”. Leave the theorem statement and proof unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source asks about positive integers, whereas Lean quantifies over all naturals and Nat.Powerful 0 is true.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The sole additional starting value is n = 0, which would require Nat.Powerful 2. This is false because 2 divides 2 but 4 does not. Thus existence of a consecutive powerful triple over ℕ is equivalent to existence with a positive starting value; their negations are equivalent as well.

reformulations.difference: Nat.nth Powerful enumerates 0, 1, 4, 8, …, and the universal quantifier includes k = 0, whereas the source enumerates positive powerful numbers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Powerful numbers form an infinite set because every square is powerful, so Nat.nth never reaches its finite-set default case. For k ≥ 1, Nat.nth Powerful k is the source’s kth positive powerful number. The extra k = 0 inequality is simply 4 > 0^c = 0 for c > 0. In scratch Lean, I proved the enumeration shift for the positive-only predicate and the equivalence of the two existential, uniform-exponent statements.

review.notes: All three theorem types faithfully state their source claims. The source explicitly records Erdős’s conjectured negative answer to the triple question and still labels the problem open. The strong variant uses real subtraction and real exponentiation, with one positive constant chosen before all indices. The textbook proof has no sorry dependency. Boundary computations and equivalence proofs compile in /workspace/review/scratch.lean; the equivalence proofs depend only on standard Lean axioms.
